topic: Zero-Mem for Pi: Zero-Token Memory Operations

primary_sources.note: Paper: Zero-Mem: Zero-Token Memory Operations for LLM Agents. Yilin Xiao, Zhehan Zhu, Yujing Zhang, Jin Chen, Zijin Hong, Luyao Zhuang, Qinggang Zhang, Shengyuan Chen, Xiaocao Ouyang, Lingfei Ren, Xiao Huang. arXiv:2607.29377v1 [cs.CL], 31 Jul 2026. License CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
Full HTML full text (fetched with curl) — used for Table 2 efficiency numbers, ablation numbers, retrieval-budget study.
HN thread (101 pts, 12 comments, 2026-08-05) — critique and community reimplementations.

competitors.title: GitHub skorotkiewicz/zero-mem — 'zero-token memory retrieval for Pi'
key_points: The repo the topic is actually about: a Pi adaptation of arXiv:2607.29377. Package/README name is 'pi-zero-mem'.

TypeScript extension (extensions/zero-mem.ts, ~41 KB) + a Python NLP worker (scripts/zero-mem-nlp.py); default branch 'dev'; ~29 commits, all 2026-08-06 to 08-08; last push 2026-08-08; low stars (~2) — very early.
Keeps Pi's original session messages as source of record; spaCy NER for entities, BGE-M3 for dense relevance, both outside any LLM call.
Implements the paper's rho = 0.6 fusion, five primary traces + bounded graph/local neighbors, provenance filtering, dedup, hybrid BM25/BGE-M3 ranking, XML escaping.
Deterministically rejects 'instruction-like' historical traces (prompt-injection guard on retrieved memory).
Pi compaction becomes a fixed non-generative checkpoint; original branch traces stay retrievable.
/zero-mem command shows retrieval route, engine, selected count, blocked historical instructions; falls back to BM25 if the Python env is missing.
Explicitly disclaims: 'Pi-oriented implementation of the architecture, not a reproduction of the paper's reported benchmark. It does not rewrite final agent answers.'

The other Pi adaptation, and the one with a launch thread of its own (Show HN: Zero-token memory retrieval for Pi, 2026-08-08, 1 point, 0 comments) - i.e. it went nowhere on distribution while remaining arguably closer to the paper's encoder choices.
Keeps Pi's original session messages as the source of record, including messages hidden by compaction, and sends only retrieved evidence plus the current turn to the reader.

Three modes: lexical-only (default, no Python, no models), semantic-only (dense spaCy + BGE-M3, reports unavailable instead of silently falling back), hybrid (combines, lexical fallback with a reported reason on NLP failure).

Adds a paper-fidelity detail zero-mem-pi lacks: deterministic rejection of instruction-like historical traces ('blocked historical instructions'), surfaced in /zero-mem output - a prompt-injection-aware retrieval filter.
Uses pi's fixed non-generative compaction checkpoint so original branch traces stay retrievable; sibling branches and the ongoing tool loop are explicitly outside the historical boundary.
Explicitly disclaims benchmark equivalence: 'this is a Pi-oriented implementation of the architecture, not a reproduction of the paper's reported benchmark.'
competitors.name: pi-zero-mem (Pi, spaCy + BGE-M3)
competitors.metrics: 2 stars, TypeScript, no license file, created 2026-08-06, last push 2026-08-08, 0 open issues

competitors.title: GitHub woolcoxm/zero-mem-pi — 'faithful reimplementation' (38★)
key_points: Second, more popular community implementation: 'Zero-token long-term memory for the pi coding agent — a faithful reimplementation of Zero-Mem (arXiv:2607.29377)'. TypeScript, 38 stars / 2 forks, created 2026-08-13, last push 2026-08-14.
Captures every finalized message as a 'trace unit' with provenance (session, project, time) + entities, embedded with bge-small-en-v1.5 (earlier MiniLM).

Routing between entity–context graph scored by Personalized PageRank (paper Eq 8–10) and a lexical/semantic view (hybrid BM25 + dense + session-adjacent turn closure, no recency prior); the paper's full temporal hierarchy is only partially realized.
Injects up to 3 snippets (default) as a '## Prior session memory' block in the system prompt; ~103 tokens/turn is the only memory token cost.

Project-scoped persistence in ~/.pi/agent/zero-mem/ (store.json + int8-quantized store.emb.bin sidecar), a derived 'identity slot' injected on first turn, retention policy (maxAgeMs/maxUnits), and a switch to pure-JS HNSW above ~10k units.
Includes a comparison table vs plain RAG and MemGPT/LLM-managed memory: 'decide what to remember' = automatic, no LLM.
Practical gotchas documented: restart pi fully (not /reload) to pick up code changes; extension can be symlinked into ~/.pi/agent/extensions/zero-mem/.

Zero-token claim: capture is passive per finalized message; retrieval is encoder + index math; the LLM is never called to decide what to remember, summarize, or forget. Only tokens spent on memory are the injected snippet (~103/turn).

Pipeline: trace unit with provenance (session, project, time) + entities; bge-small-en-v1.5 embeddings in an int8-quantized sidecar (store.emb.bin); coverage router over BM25 + dense; entity-context graph scored by Personalized PageRank (paper Eq 8-10, gamma=0.6) as primary view at rho=0.6; evidence closure over graph bridges and session-adjacent local spans; deterministic calibration.

Injects up to 3 snippets (default) capped at 120 chars each as a '## Prior session memory' block in the system prompt; the full temporal hierarchy of the paper is only partially realized (README concedes this).

Sticky identity slot: agent and user names derived deterministically from the store, persisted in store.json so retention cannot evict them, injected on every session's first turn and on identity-class queries.

Retention bounds growth (ZERO_MEM_MAX_UNITS default 2000, ZERO_MEM_MAX_AGE_DAYS default 90); above ~10k embedded units retrieval switches from exact brute-force cosine to pure-JS HNSW with a growth-gated rebuild.

Storage and perf numbers measured live on a 236-unit store (dim 384) at 94.77 tok/s prompt-eval: store on disk 2088 KB -> 239 KB (-88%); load 45.2 ms -> 8.7 ms; persist 93.4 ms -> 20.9 ms; capture 0.04 ms; retrieve 5.1 ms semantic / 1.3 ms BM25-only; injection 276 -> 103 tok/turn (-173), i.e. ~1825 ms less prefill per turn against ~20 s of base system-prompt and tools prefill.

Publishes its own negative and neutral results: graph is metric-neutral at retrieval level (identical hard-negative scores with graph off) and neutral at reader level too; evidence calibration helped retrieval MRR (0.396 -> 0.404) while HURTING the reader (-3.4 F1 pts) and was then made tie-only in v0.14f.

Install is git-clone plus `pi -e <Windows path>\index.ts`; there is no npm package (zero-mem-pi, @woolcoxm/zero-mem-pi, pi-zero-mem all 404 on the registry) and the README's quickstart still hardcodes C:\Users\Robot\projects\zero-mem-pi.

Status header lists five live-bug hotfixes between v0.14b and v0.14h, all shipped 2026-08-14: weak-pool injection, cross-project identity, quotation-vs-statement ranking, typo/'go by' naming phrasings, and finally the harness-default poison filter.

competitors.title: HN discussion — 'Zero-Mem: Zero-Token Memory Operations for LLM Agents' (101 pts)
key_points: Top critique (russlan): the contribution is not zero token cost, it is removing generative rewriting from memory — preserving original traces avoids the auditability failure where retrieval is grounded in a summary's omissions rather than the evidence.

Wants a harder benchmark around mutation and contradiction: if an entity's attributes change across sessions, can the graph + temporal hierarchy preserve both states, surface the conflict, and show which trace justified the answer? Argues production agents should be measured on unsupported-answer rate and evidence recall under stale/conflicting/adversarial traces.
langs: alternative approach — store the conversation's KV cache locally and retrieve on attention scores; reports SOTA on LoCoMo and LongMemEval (github.com/AttemorySystem/attemory).
kolinko: similar system, ~0.3 s retrieval over a few million pre-chunked tokens, but needed ~200 GB RAM/VRAM for cached KVs.
elij + jackdawed: 'easy to implement at the harness level and the NER can be way more naive' — jackdawed claims a clean-room Rust implementation (github.com/ptaranat/zeromem).
Takeaway for the article: the community consensus is that the interesting claim is auditability/no-generation, not the token savings alone.

competitors.title: Tandemly Research — 'Zero-Mem: Agent Memory Without the Model Call'
key_points: Best framing of the paper's thesis: write-time summarization calls and read-time retrieval-scoring calls 'look like a data structure problem' — so replace generation with deterministic structure.
Names the core result: 57.6% lower memory-operation time cost vs the fastest baseline at matched final-answer quality, zero LLM tokens on memory operations, model called once (final answer).
Notes at time of writing that the reference code release is pending peer review; points readers to woolcoxm/zero-mem-pi as the community implementation.

competitors.title: Sesame Disk — 'Zero-Token Memory for Scalable LLM Agents' (Aug 5, 2026)
key_points: Frames the 'memory token bill' with third-party numbers (via VentureBeat): LangMem ~3.26M tokens per session; xMemory ~118k tokens per query.
Explains Zero-Mem by contrast with summarization-based memory and warns that production adoption is nascent.

Weakness to avoid in our article: it pads Zero-Mem with an unrelated MatMul-free-architecture section and its key-takeaway box is self-contradictory (says 'decouple memory management from token consumption' then talks about GPU memory in GB). Good example of what NOT to write.

competitors.name: zeromem (Rust, Hermes Agent memory provider)
competitors.metrics: 15 stars, 2 forks, Rust, MIT, created 2026-08-05, last push 2026-08-24, 17 commits
key_points: Closest sibling implementation: a from-the-paper Rust crate with a zm CLI, a PyO3 Python module, and a Hermes Agent memory provider plugin (memory.provider: zeromem), plus a Claude Code integration.

Maps every paper equation to a module (eq 3-4 graph/ner.rs, eq 6-7 profile/route.rs, eq 8-10 PPR graph_view.rs, eq 12-13 fuse.rs, eq 14 closure.rs, eq 15-16 calibrate.rs) and states its deviations explicitly: heuristic NER instead of spaCy, bge-small-en-v1.5 via fastembed instead of BGE-M3, deterministic hash embedder as offline fallback.

Ships as a single SQLite file where graph, hierarchy and BM25 rebuild from turns on open, so the store cannot drift from its indexes - a stronger storage-integrity claim than zero-mem-pi's derived indexes.

README was written by reading the paper ('clean-room implementation') before the reference code existed; the HN thread produced at least two such independent implementations in different languages within days.

Illustrates that the zero-token regime is portable infrastructure, not a product: the same paper produced a Pi extension, a Rust crate with a Hermes provider, and a Claude Code skill in the same five weeks.

competitors.name: ZeroMem (Claude Code skill, zero dependencies)
competitors.metrics: 9 stars, 1 fork, Python 3.12+, MIT, created 2026-08-06, last push 2026-09-05, 59 commits
key_points: Indexes the user's own Claude Code transcripts (~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl) and returns evidence with no LLM call anywhere in the memory pipeline - enforced, not asserted: tests/test_no_llm_calls.py fails the build if any module imports an HTTP client or names an LLM API.

Zero new dependencies (numpy, scipy, regex): BM25 vendored on scipy.sparse, nearest-neighbour as a numpy matmul, entity extraction by regex; dense encoder tiers (~2 GB torch wheels) are strictly opt-in.

Adds things the paper does not have and measures them: an abstention support gate that names missing terms, a targeted probe on weak results, and a local recall daemon that loads the index once for ~18x faster warm recall.
Most active of the from-paper implementations (59 commits through 2026-09-05, including a tool-effect policy and a coordination ledger) - the opposite maintenance profile to zero-mem-pi.
Shows the portability ceiling is low: the paper's four components can be re-created in a few weeks by one developer against a different harness's transcripts.

competitors.name: pi-observational-memory (the pi incumbent on token-aware memory)
competitors.metrics: 672 stars, 93 forks, TypeScript, MIT, created 2026-04-14, last push 2026-09-29, 7,667 npm downloads/month
key_points: The extension pi users actually adopt for memory ('Make Pi sessions feel endless'): cache-friendly tiered compaction with observations and reflections, i.e. LLM-driven memory management - exactly the regime Zero-Mem argues against.
Its premise is that compaction is the problem, not retrieval: it spends tokens to keep a session coherent rather than spending tokens to recall across sessions.
29x more GitHub stars and 7.7k downloads/month versus zero-mem-pi's 38 stars and no npm presence - the adoption gap, not the architecture, is the story for a pi memory review.
Useful contrast axis for the article: LLM-compress-and-keep-working (observational memory) vs never-compress-and-recall-deterministically (zero-mem).

competitors.name: claude-mem (and pi-agent-memory, its pi adaptation)
competitors.metrics: claude-mem 95,021 stars / 8,409 forks / Apache-2.0 / TypeScript, 73,866 npm downloads/month; pi-agent-memory fork: 190 downloads/month, AGPL-3.0
key_points: The mainstream design Zero-Mem defines itself against: capture everything the agent does, compress it with AI, inject relevant context into future sessions.

Its pi adaptation (pi-agent-memory) is a fork-and-adaptation that connects pi to claude-mem's worker service for cross-session, cross-engine memory with hybrid search (FTS5 + Chroma vector embeddings) - meaning the pi ecosystem's default answer to memory is an LLM compressor, not a deterministic retriever.
95k stars is the scale of the category leader; a zero-token extension competes with that gravitational pull on trust, not on features.
AGPL-3.0 on the pi fork is worth flagging for commercial readers - a licensing difference that affects adoption independent of technical merit.

competitors.name: agentmemory (the token-efficient commercial middle ground)
competitors.metrics: 29.1K installs claimed on site, v0.9.29, 'Linux Foundation backed', 54 MCP tools / 134 REST endpoints, no external databases
key_points: Claims 95.2% retrieval R@5 on LongMemEval-S at ~92% fewer input tokens than full-context replay, with hybrid BM25 + vector + knowledge-graph reranking on the device - the honest counterexample that deterministic retrieval quality and low token cost are not mutually exclusive.
Consolidation 'with an LLM provider key' runs on session stop, so it is a hybrid regime (deterministic recall path, optional generative consolidation) rather than the strict zero-token posture.
12 auto-capture hooks into every coding agent, superseded versions suppressed from results, lifecycle decay and audit rows - the features a production buyer asks for that zero-mem-pi does not have.

Independent blog measurements put Mem0 at 94.4 on LongMemEval at roughly 6,900 tokens per query, versus no-model systems like deja at 85.3% LongMemEval-S - the accuracy-vs-token-cost tradeoff is real and public, which is the frame a Zero-Mem review should use.

competitors.name: Zero-Mem: Zero-Token Memory Operations for LLM Agents (the paper)
competitors.metrics: arXiv:2607.29377v1, cs.CL, 31 Jul 2026; Yilin Xiao et al., HK PolyU + SWUFE + Jilin; HN 101 points / 12 comments; reference code at github.com/TheMoon0815/Zero-mem (and Zero-Mem/Zero-mem, 93 stars) withheld until after peer review; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license on the HTML
key_points: Defines zero-token memory operations as a regime: memory construction, organization, routing, retrieval, evidence closure, pre-reader evidence calibration and post-reader answer calibration invoke no LLM and consume no LLM input/output tokens; encoder computation and final-QA inference are accounted for separately.
Four components: provenance-preserving token-free memory substrate, query-conditioned evidence routing, dual-view evidence retrieval and closure, deterministic evidence calibration.

Reader-level results with GPT-4o-mini: LoCoMo average F1 59.15 / BLEU-1 52.96 vs GAM 53.75 / 47.51 (best baseline) - +5.40 / +5.45 points; HotpotQA F1 72.07 / 66.43 / 65.04 at 56K / 224K / 448K vs GAM 63.22 / 64.56 / 59.81.

Efficiency table: 0 memory-operation tokens vs LightMem's 877,086 (the most token-efficient baseline) and GAM's 28,570,674; 334.77 s total / 0.22 s per query; -57.6% memory-operation latency vs the fastest baseline, with matched final-QA reader and context budget.

Ablations on HotpotQA (56K, GPT-4o-mini): full 72.07 F1, graph-only 62.50, hierarchy-only 54.88, closure removed 67.90, calibration removed 70.13 - i.e. both structural views are load-bearing at reader level.

Retrieval budget sensitivity on LoCoMo: F1 52.59 at top-1 -> 59.15 at top-5 -> best at top-10, stable beyond; all methods capped at five retrieved items for a controlled comparison; gamma and rho both 0.6; RTX 4090 hardware.

The paper's own caveat that makes the pi port's numbers interpretable: 'zero-token operation does not imply zero computation' - encoder inference, memory organization, retrieval and calibration still cost time.

stats.fact: Zero-Mem consumes zero LLM input/output tokens for memory operations and 0 ms of memory-operation overhead; GAM (strongest quality baseline) burned 28,570,674 memory tokens and 18,552.39 s total overhead; LightMem (the most token-efficient baseline) still burned 877,086 tokens.
stats.source: arXiv:2607.29377v1, Table 2 (efficiency comparison, GPT-4o-mini, same concurrency/hardware)

stats.fact: Total memory-operation time 334.77 s and 0.22 s per query vs LightMem's 788.76 s / 0.51 s — a 57.6% latency reduction versus the fastest baseline.

In the same efficiency setting Zero-Mem also posts the best quality: 59.15 F1 / 52.96 BLEU-1, i.e. +10.0% F1 and +11.5% BLEU-1 over GAM — 'eliminating LLM-based memory operations does not compromise answer quality'.

LoCoMo: Zero-Mem gets the best average F1 and BLEU-1 under both readers, +5.40 F1 / +5.45 BLEU-1 over GAM (strongest overall baseline) with GPT-4o-mini (59.15/52.96 avg) and +4.87/+4.86 with Qwen2.5-14B (57.57/51.41 avg).
stats.source: arXiv:2607.29377v1, Table 1 (LoCoMo: single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain)

stats.fact: HotpotQA: highest F1 across all readers as context grows from 56K to 448K tokens, average +5.52 points F1 over the strongest baseline.

Ablation (HotpotQA, 56K context, GPT-4o-mini): full model 72.07 F1 / 69.66 BLEU-1; graph view only 62.50/59.90; hierarchy only 54.88/51.40; no evidence closure 67.90/65.43; no calibration 70.13/66.45 — the two views are complementary, with the graph doing the heavy lifting on HotpotQA.
Retrieval budget: performance improves markedly from top-1 to top-5, best average at top-10, then stable; the paper uses top-5 to match baseline retrieval settings.
stats.source: arXiv:2607.29377v1, Figure 4 (Effect of the Retrieval Budget)

stats.fact: Default parameters to cite: gamma 0.6, rho 0.6, top-5 evidence (paper defaults, mirrored in the Rust port).

Pi has no memory model at all: it is a branchable session substrate (JSONL session tree that forks/clones, deterministic file manifests on compaction, 20+ ExtensionAPI lifecycle events). Searching its SDK docs for 'memory' returns only SessionManager.inMemory()/InMemoryCredentialStore — storage backends, not agent memory. Memory plugins must build everything on top of context / session_start / session_before_compact.

The pi-adaptation repo has ~2 stars and 0 issues while the parallel 'faithful reimplementation' has 38 stars — the ecosystem is tiny and fragmented; adjacent pi memory options are pi-mem (~79★, plain Markdown, no embeddings), pi-memory (npm, semantic search via qmd), Magic Context, pi-agent-memory.
stats.source: GitHub API (repos: skorotkiewicz/zero-mem, woolcoxm/zero-mem-pi, jo-inc/pi-mem) + pi.dev package directory

stats.fact: Agent-memory token costs in the wider field: LangMem ~3.26M tokens per session, xMemory ~118k tokens per query — the 'memory token bill' Zero-Mem attacks.
stats.source: VentureBeat numbers as relayed by sesamedisk.com (Aug 5, 2026) — secondary, attribute to VentureBeat

stats.fact: Zero-Mem's headline efficiency result: 0 LLM tokens consumed on memory operations (vs 877,086 for LightMem, the most token-efficient baseline, and 28,570,674 for GAM), 334.77 s total and 0.22 s per query on the same hardware, a 57.6% reduction in memory-operation latency against the fastest baseline at matched reader and context budget.

Answer quality with a GPT-4o-mini reader: Zero-Mem 59.15 F1 / 52.96 BLEU-1 on LoCoMo, +10.0% and +11.5% over GAM, the second-best method; with Qwen2.5-14B it is 64.09 / 58.19 on the average and first on every question type.
HotpotQA F1 by context length (GPT-4o-mini / Qwen2.5-14B): Zero-Mem 72.07 / 68.58 at 56K, 66.43 / 65.47 at 224K, 65.04 / 61.02 at 448K, versus GAM at 63.22 / 64.07, 64.56 / 55.99 and 59.81 / 57.87.

Ablation on HotpotQA at 56K with GPT-4o-mini: full model 72.07 F1 / 69.66 BLEU-1; graph view only 62.50 / 59.90; hierarchical view only 54.88 / 51.40; without evidence closure 67.90 / 65.43; without evidence calibration 70.13 / 66.45.

Retrieval budget sensitivity on LoCoMo: average F1/BLEU-1 rise from 52.59 / 46.79 at top-1 to 59.15 / 52.96 at top-5, peak at top-10, then stay stable; single-hop questions saturate early while multi-hop, temporal and open-domain keep benefiting from more evidence.
stats.source: https://arxiv.org/html/2607.29377v1 (Effect of the Retrieval Budget, Figure 4)

stats.fact: The paper's reference implementation was NOT released with the paper: 'After peer review, the code and implementation details will be available at https://github.com/TheMoon0815/Zero-mem' - the org repo (93 stars, created 2026-07-30) still contains no code. The HTML is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

At least ten independent Zero-Mem implementations exist within five weeks, in at least four languages/harnesses: ptaranat/zeromem (Rust + Hermes provider, 15 stars), viethuynh243/ZeroMem (Claude Code skill, 9 stars), woolcoxm/zero-mem-pi (Pi, 38 stars), skorotkiewicz/zero-mem (Pi, 2 stars), sarsvankelsion/zero-mem and sarsed-code, jlucasrods/zeromem-opencode, SJT503/Claude-zero-mem, droxey/nebula-zero-mem, plus a Pi-adjacent A.I.M. zero-token exoskeleton. A GitHub repository search for the term returns total_count 66 (mostly unrelated ZeroMemory projects).
stats.source: GitHub REST API search/repositories?q="zero-mem" OR "zero token memory" OR zeromem (2026-09-30) + per-repo GET /repos

stats.fact: Subject repo metrics at research time: woolcoxm/zero-mem-pi - 38 stars, 2 forks, 0 open issues, TypeScript, MIT, created 2026-08-13, last push 2026-08-14, 42 commits (v0.5 through v0.14h).

The extension was published to GitHub but not to npm: registry lookups for zero-mem-pi, @woolcoxm/zero-mem-pi, pi-zero-mem and zero-mem all return 404, and the README quickstart still points at C:\Users\Robot\projects\zero-mem-pi with `pi -e <path>\index.ts`.

Self-measured storage/efficiency numbers on a real 236-unit store (dim 384) at 94.77 tok/s prompt-eval: store 2088 KB -> 239 KB (-88%) after int8 sidecar quantization; load 45.2 -> 8.7 ms; persist 93.4 -> 20.9 ms; capture 0.04 ms; retrieve 5.1 ms semantic (with query embed) and 1.3 ms BM25-only; injection 276 -> 103 tokens/turn, i.e. -1825 ms prefill per turn against ~20 s of base prefill.

Retrieval eval, LoCoMo10 (10 conversations, 1986 QA), recall@5 / MRR: BM25 only 0.535 / 0.399; pure semantic MiniLM 0.273 / 0.183; pure semantic bge-small 0.427 / 0.296; RRF hybrid 0.552 / 0.384; coverage fusion + PPR graph (v0.14) 0.546 / 0.404. Paired McNemar: 31 CORE-only hits vs 9 BM25-only, p ~ 0.0009.

Held-out honesty: the coverage fusion beats BM25 by +0.015 on the tuning half of LoCoMo (convs 1-5) but only +0.007 on the untouched half (convs 6-10, 0.531 vs 0.524) - roughly half the headline gap is tuned-on-test bias, per the author's own split.

Structural views are metric-neutral in the author's own evals: closure off gives identical LoCoMo recall@5 (0.546 / 0.403) and the graph is identical on the 200-fact hard-negative eval; at reader level (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, 100-QA seeded sample) the graph is neutral (F1 0.099 vs 0.098 full), closure is +0.8 F1 pts, and flat evidence calibration is NEGATIVE (-3.4 pts, 0.132 without it) though a paired test says directional not decisive (p=0.093, EM p=0.5, hit@10 identical).

The port's end-to-end reader numbers are far below the paper's: answer F1 0.200 / EM 0.040 / BLEU-1 0.224 on a 50-QA LoCoMo sample with a Qwen3-Coder reader (hit@10 0.40), and F1 0.098-0.136 / EM 0.050-0.070 on a 100-QA sample with Qwen2.5-14B - versus 59.15 F1 in the paper, which uses a GPT-4o-mini reader, different prompt protocol and a different sample. The README labels its own number a lower bound, not a comparable result.

Paraphrase and hard-negative retrieval evals: BM25-only 0.75 recall@5 vs coverage fusion + PPR 0.96 on the 24-fact paraphrase set (MRR 0.74 -> 0.90); on the 200-fact hard-negative set (each fact with a one-value-different sibling) BM25 0.682, dense-only + graph 0.647, coverage fusion + PPR 0.695 - a real but small +0.013 margin.

Default retention and injection configuration: ZERO_MEM_MAX_UNITS 2000, ZERO_MEM_MAX_AGE_DAYS 90, ZERO_MEM_INJECT_TOPK 3 (on-demand /memory and recall_memory use 8), ZERO_MEM_INJECT_SNIPPET 120 chars, ZERO_MEM_HNSW_THRESHOLD 10000. HNSW recall@10 vs exact brute force is 90-96% at ef=200 (dim 384), and HNSW stays dormant below 10k units because brute force is both faster and exact there.

The paper's HN thread (2026-08-05) reached 101 points and 12 comments; the top technical critique was that the durable contribution is removing generative rewriting rather than saving tokens, because once an LLM compresses an interaction, retrieval is grounded in the summary's omissions rather than the evidence.
stats.source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49178608 (HN Algolia item API, comment by russlan)

stats.fact: Pi's own architecture makes the recall case: sessions are stored under ~/.pi/agent/sessions/ grouped by working directory, and compaction 'adds a summary and keeps recent messages. It does not delete the original session entries' - so pre-compaction detail survives on disk and can be retrieved deterministically.

Independent measurement of how lossy compaction is: across 43 compactions the surviving summary retained 77% of decisions but only 0.2% of commands - 99.8% of concrete, actionable command history disappeared from the live context (recoverable by re-indexing the pre-compaction transcripts).
stats.source: Internal: our own post /home/ubuntu/blog/content/posts/deja-vu-memory-coding-agents-indexes-sessions.md (2026-09-15), citing deja's compaction study

stats.fact: Same source, for the token-cost frame: full-context injection scores 46.20% on LongMemEval while a no-memory baseline falls to 22.8%, and Mem0 reaches 94.4 on LongMemEval at roughly 6,900 tokens per query - the accuracy-vs-token-cost curve any Zero-Mem adoption decision sits on.

Ecosystem scale that dwarfs the subject: claude-mem (the LLM-compressing memory system Zero-Mem argues against) has 95,021 stars, 8,409 forks and 73,866 npm downloads/month; agentmemory advertises 29.1K installs with 95.2% R@5 on LongMemEval-S at ~92% fewer input tokens.

The pi memory-extension market the article should compare against, by monthly npm downloads / stars: billion-context-pi 64,336; @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents 49,910; pi-memory 36,008 (178 stars); memorix 28,461; pi-hermes-memory 22,096 (467 stars); gentle-engram 18,338; pi-observational-memory 7,667 (672 stars); pi-continual-harness 914; nowledge-mem-pi 840; pi-dense-mem 384. For context @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent itself is 11,307,759/month.

Measured search demand (Google/YouTube autocomplete, 2026-09-30): 'zero mem pi agent' returns NO suggestions; 'zero token memory agent' and 'coding agent memory zero tokens' return none; 'zero token memory' returns only itself; 'zero-mem pi' returns an unrelated Polish phrase. By contrast 'pi agent memory' returns a full cluster (extension, plugin, persistent memory, observational memory, memory system, reddit) and 'pi coding agent memory' returns the same cluster plus 'memory md'. The topic's demand is in the generic pi-memory phrase, not in 'zero mem'.

The subject's launch was covered by release aggregators within hours (KBlip, 2026-08-13, 'Zero-Mem brings zero-token memory to pi coding agent', 34 engagement, 1 source) and the paper by a research synthesis page (Tandemly, 2026-08-05) - meaning the category has PR-style coverage but almost no user reports, issue threads or reviews.

angles: 'Zero-token' is a scope claim, not a magic claim: Zero-Mem eliminates LLM calls and LLM tokens from memory operations only — encoder inference, indexing, retrieval and calibration still cost compute (334.77 s for the whole run). Explaining this precisely is the fastest way to be more useful than the aggregator posts.

The real headline is auditability, not cost: raw traces stay the source of record, so retrieval is grounded in evidence instead of a summary's omissions. HN's top comment makes this point better than the abstract does.

The gap nobody has covered: the paper benchmarked LoCoMo/HotpotQA QA workloads, but a pi user's problem is code sessions — compaction, branch switching, 'what did I decide three sessions ago'. The pi ports are architectural adaptations, not reproductions, and both say so in their READMEs.

Concrete, verifiable differences between the two pi ports: skorotkiewicz = spaCy + BGE-M3 in a Python worker with BM25 fallback and an instruction-trace rejection filter; woolcoxm = compromise NER + bge-small-en-v1.5 + int8 embeddings + HNSW, partial temporal hierarchy, identity slot.

Honest limitation section: no peer-reviewed code release yet (coming after review), mutation/contradiction handling unproven, stale/conflicting evidence recall unmeasured, ~1-2 stars of real-world mileage, and Pi's missing memory contract (no deletion hook, no scope) is inherited by every plugin.

Pi-specific mechanics make the article useful: where traces come from (session tree incl. sibling branches and messages hidden by compaction), why pi compaction is turned into a fixed non-generative checkpoint, and the /zero-mem inspection command.

Cost framing for a coding agent: the only memory tokens spent are the injected snippet (~103 tokens/turn in woolcoxm's default of 3 snippets), versus per-turn or per-query LLM maintenance calls in LLM-managed memory systems.

Lead the review with the honesty, not the headline. The repo's own evals say the measurable win is coverage fusion (BM25+dense blended by lexical coverage), not the paper's structural views: the PPR graph is metric-neutral at both retrieval and reader level, evidence closure is worth about +0.8 F1 points at reader level, and flat evidence calibration was NEGATIVE at reader level (-3.4 pts) before being made tie-only. A review that reports 0.546 r@5 as if it were the paper's 59.15 F1 is the failure mode to avoid - and the author says so in the README.

Five live bugs in roughly 24 hours, four of them identity/amnesia failures, is the most concrete thing in the repo. The best one is v0.14h: the agent self-named 'Aio' and 41 seconds later answered 'whats your name?' with 'You can call me Pi' - because pi's own default reply is 'call me X'-shaped and was ingested as self-naming evidence. The memory system was injecting the agent's amnesia. That is a quotable, generalizable failure mode for any trace-preserving memory design.

The reader gap is the open question the article should hold open rather than resolve: 0.098-0.200 answer F1 in the port's own strict-RAG harness vs 59.15 in the paper with a GPT-4o-mini reader, different protocol and different sample. The README names the missing experiment (reader-F1 ablations that can credit or retire the structural views). Report that as the state of the evidence.

At least ten independent reimplementations in five weeks, in Rust, Python and TypeScript, across Pi, Claude Code, Hermes and opencode - while the paper's own repo withholds code 'after peer review'. The zero-token regime is cheap to reimplement and the reference is absent, so every comparison in this space is implementation-vs-paper, not implementation-vs-implementation. That is a structural reason to distrust any 'beats Zero-Mem' claim, including the port's.

The real competitor is not a rival implementation; it is the LLM-compressing pi ecosystem. pi-observational-memory (672 stars, 7.7k downloads/month), pi-memory (37.1k/month), billion-context-pi (64.3k/month), pi-hermes-memory (467 stars, 22.1k/month) and claude-mem-derived pi-agent-memory all spend tokens on memory and get adopted anyway. Zero-token is a property almost nobody has asked for yet - which is the honest business read on a 38-star repo with no npm package.

Why it matters in pi specifically: pi keeps session files on disk and its compaction 'does not delete the original session entries', so pre-compaction evidence is still there to be retrieved deterministically. Our own published measurement of compaction loss (77% of decisions survive but only 0.2% of commands) is the concrete harm this architecture addresses - and zero-mem-pi addresses it at ~103 injected tokens per turn, without an index server or an MCP call.

The token-vs-latency trade is the practical lever for pi readers, who disproportionately run local models. At the author's measured 94.77 tok/s prompt-eval rate, cutting injection from 276 to 103 tokens saves about 1,825 ms of prefill per turn against ~20 s of base prefill - but retrieval still costs 5.1 ms per turn and every message still gets embedded. Zero-token is not zero-cost; the paper says so ('zero-token operation does not imply zero computation') and so does the port.

Storage engineering is the underrated part: int8-quantized embedding sidecar cut the store from 2,088 KB to 239 KB (-88%), load from 45.2 to 8.7 ms and persist from 93.4 to 20.9 ms, and pure-JS HNSW is deliberately kept dormant below 10k units because exact brute force is faster AND exact there. These are the details someone porting this would actually reuse.

Determinism as an audit property survives even if the token savings turn out to be modest: same query plus same store yields the same retrieval set, there is no sampling variance, and every unit keeps its source session/time metadata. For teams who need to explain why an agent recalled something, that is a stronger claim than 'it uses fewer tokens'.

The maintenance and distribution profile is the practical caution: 38 stars, 0 open issues, no commits since 2026-08-14, no npm package (all candidate names 404), and a README quickstart that hardcodes a Windows path. Compare with viethuynh243/ZeroMem (59 commits, still active) and ptaranat/zeromem (race-safe hooks, changelog) - if a reader wants to run the architecture, the Rust crate with the Hermes provider or the Claude Code skill is currently the more maintained path.

Privacy posture is the quiet differentiator worth one section: everything lives under ~/.pi/agent/zero-mem/ with no cloud, no API key and no embedding vendor, versus the cloud-backed pi options (@mem0/pi-agent-plugin, pi-memory-honcho/Honcho). For anyone working in a private repo with a local model, that combination - local traces, local encoder, deterministic retrieval - is the actual reason to care, more than the token count.

Search demand tells you how to frame it: 'zero mem pi agent' has zero autocomplete suggestions while 'pi agent memory' / 'pi coding agent memory' return a rich cluster (extension, plugin, persistent memory, observational memory). Win the generic pi-memory and brand terms, and use 'zero-token' as the differentiator inside the piece - not as the primary keyword.

summary: Zero-Mem for pi (woolcoxm/zero-mem-pi) is a 38-star, MIT-licensed TypeScript extension that gives the pi coding agent long-term memory without spending any LLM call or token on memory operations - a faithful reimplementation of Zero-Mem (arXiv:2607.29377, Hong Kong Polytechnic University / SWUFE / Jilin, 101 points on HN 2026-08-05). It captures every finalized message as a provenance-bearing trace unit, embeds it with bge-small-en-v1.5 into an int8 sidecar, and on each prompt runs a zero-LLM retrieval pipeline: a coverage router blends BM25 and dense scores, an entity-context graph scored by Personalized PageRank is fused in as the primary view (rho=0.6), evidence closure follows graph bridges and local neighbors, deterministic calibration filters the set, and up to 3 snippets (~103 tokens/turn) are injected as a '## Prior session memory' block. The honest evidence position is the story: the author's own retrieval evals show the measurable win comes from coverage fusion (LoCoMo10 r@5 0.546 vs BM25 0.535, McNemar 31-vs-9 p~0.0009; paraphrase eval 0.96 vs 0.75; hard-negative 0.695 vs 0.682) while the paper's structural views - PPR graph and evidence closure - are metric-NEUTRAL at retrieval level and only weakly positive at reader level (closure +0.8 F1 pts, graph neutral); the README itself says the open experiment is reader-F1 ablations. End-to-end reader F1 in its own strict-RAG harness is 0.098-0.136 against the paper's 59.15 with a GPT-4o-mini reader, so the review must not present 0.546 r@5 and 59.15 F1 as the same claim. Operationally the repo shipped 42 commits in roughly 24 hours (2026-08-13 to 08-14) fixing five consecutive live bugs - four of them identity/amnesia failures, the last caused by the harness's own default reply ('you can just call me Pi') being ingested as self-naming evidence. The competitive reality is two-sided: at least ten independent zero-token reimplementations appeared within five weeks (ptaranat/zeromem in Rust with a Hermes provider, viethuynh243/ZeroMem for Claude Code, skorotkiewicz/zero-mem for pi, plus smaller ones; GitHub search returns 66 repos) while the paper's own repo withholds code pending peer review - but the adoption that matters is in the pi memory-extension ecosystem, where LLM-compressing extensions like pi-memory (37.1k downloads/month), billion-context-pi (64.3k), pi-observational-memory (672 stars, 7.7k/mo), pi-hermes-memory (467 stars, 22.1k/mo) and claude-mem-derived pi-agent-memory have orders of magnitude more users. Verdict framing for the article: zero-mem-pi is the only pi memory extension whose memory path provably makes no LLM calls and the only one that publishes its own negative results - and it is also the least maintained, unpublished to npm, uninstallable without editing a Windows path, and dormant since 2026-08-14. Read it for the architecture and the honesty; do not depend on it yet.

supplemental_findings.a: It means no step outside final question answering invokes an LLM or consumes LLM input/output tokens: capture, organization, query routing, retrieval, evidence closure and evidence calibration are all deterministic encoder and index math. Encoder computation is accounted for separately, so 'zero-token' does not mean free - the pi port still embeds every finalized message and spends about 5.1 ms per prompt on retrieval.

supplemental_findings.q: How many tokens does it add to each turn?
supplemental_findings.a: The pi extension injects up to 3 snippets capped at 120 characters each, measured at roughly 103 tokens per turn (down from ~276 in the earlier top-5 x 220-char configuration) - about 1,825 ms less prefill per turn at a 94.77 tok/s prompt-eval rate. On-demand /memory and the optional recall_memory tool use 8 snippets instead.

supplemental_findings.q: Does it beat vector search in the author's own tests?
supplemental_findings.a: On paraphrase-style queries, yes clearly (0.96 vs 0.75 recall@5). On real LoCoMo conversational lookups, the honest answer is narrowly: coverage fusion scores 0.546 vs BM25's 0.535 (McNemar p ~ 0.0009, and +0.007 on the untouched held-out conversation split), and pure dense is worse than BM25 there (0.427 with bge-small, 0.273 with MiniLM). The win comes from blending BM25 with dense by lexical coverage, not from the entity graph - the graph is metric-neutral in these retrieval evals.

supplemental_findings.q: Why is its reader F1 so much lower than the paper's?
supplemental_findings.a: Because it is a different experiment. The paper reports end-to-end answer F1 with a GPT-4o-mini reader under its own prompt protocol and sample (59.15 on LoCoMo); the pi port runs a strict RAG setup with a local reader (Qwen3-Coder or Qwen2.5-14B) on 50-100 question samples and gets 0.098-0.200 F1 at hit@10 0.4-0.6. The README labels its number a lower bound, and names the reader-F1 ablations as the open experiment.

It is MIT-licensed, local-only, and writes to ~/.pi/agent/zero-mem/. But it is not on npm (every candidate package name returns 404), the README quickstart hardcodes a Windows path, there have been no commits since 2026-08-14, and five live bugs - four of them identity/amnesia failures - were fixed inside a single 24-hour burst. Treat it as a readable, runnable research artifact rather than a dependency, and note the project's own warning that pi extensions run with the same OS permissions as pi itself.

supplemental_findings.q: How is it different from pi-observational-memory or pi-memory?
supplemental_findings.a: Those spend LLM calls on memory: observational memory compresses observations and reflections into cache-friendly tiers so long sessions stay coherent, and pi-memory writes durable facts plus optional qmd-powered semantic search. Zero-Mem refuses generation entirely - it stores raw traces and retrieves deterministically - and it is currently two to three orders of magnitude behind them on adoption (38 stars and no npm package vs 672 stars / 7.7k downloads a month and 178 stars / 37.1k downloads a month).

supplemental_findings.q: What is the most useful thing to take away even if I never install it?
supplemental_findings.a: Two ideas. First, audit your memory pipeline for model calls that are doing RETRIEVAL work dressed up as generation - write-time summarization and read-time relevance scoring are usually matching jobs a data structure can do. Second, note the failure in v0.14h: the agent's memory was injecting its own default answer ('call me Pi') as self-naming evidence, which is what trace-preserving memory buys you - it preserves your mistakes faithfully, so your ingestion filters have to be as careful as your retrieval.
